subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage:
Dear Vijay,
I am writing this instead of asking you across the dinner table, since I know you hate that. As your parent, I've noticed you turn your phone face down when I walk in, and you have been quieter. You are allowed privacy; I had some at your age too, and I trust you.
I am not asking you to show me anything. I would just like to know that you are okay. If you want to tell me about something that's on your mind, I will listen first and not lecture. And one thing is non-negotiable: if anyone online ever asks you to keep a secret from me or to meet in person, please tell me straight away. I will never be angry about that.
Love,
Tanvir

qa.q: How does Tanvir describe Vijay's behaviour when Tanvir walks in?
qa.a: Vijay turns the phone face down when Tanvir walks in.

qa.q: What is Tanvir worried about while writing the letter?
qa.a: Tanvir is anxious about Vijay's quietness and secrecy, and wants to know Vijay is okay. Writing instead of asking across the table shows care not to interrogate.

qa.q: What in the letter matches worry with respect for privacy?
qa.a: Tanvir says privacy is allowed, does not ask to see anything and promises to listen without lecturing. The clear safety expectation is to tell Tanvir if anyone online asks for a secret or a meeting.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Vijay might feel relieved not to be interrogated and trusted with privacy. The promise not to be angry may make it easier to speak up if something is wrong.

grounding: A parent senses a teenager's secrecy and writes a letter that respects privacy while asking open questions and setting clear safety expectations.

subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage:
Let me tell you about the winter I spent being a detective, and failing. I'm Vandana. My son Harish, fifteen, started hiding his phone, and going quiet. I panicked. One night I fired ten questions at him: "Who is that? Show me the messages, what is this app?" Harish went silent and shut his door.
The next evening, chopping onions, I said, "I noticed you've been quiet. Anything you want to tell me? No pressure." Silence, and then, "There's a group I like. Just friends." I said, "Okay. One thing: if anyone ever asks you to keep secrets from me, or to meet, you tell me and I won't be angry."
He nodded. I felt small and relieved. We're still working on it.

qa.q: How many questions did Vandana fire at Harish one night?
qa.a: Vandana fired ten questions at Harish.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling when Harish started hiding the phone and going quiet?
qa.a: Vandana was panicked and worried. Firing ten questions came from fear, not from a wish to control.

qa.q: What did Vandana do differently the next evening, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Vandana asked one open question while chopping onions, with no pressure, and set one clear safety rule. Harish then said there was a group of friends he liked.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt when ten questions arrived at once?
qa.a: Harish probably felt cornered and defensive, which is why he shut his door. A single gentle question the next evening let him breathe and answer.

grounding: A person senses secrecy in their teenage son, first interrogates and then uses an open question and a clear safety rule.

subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage:
I'm Usha, Manoj's elder sister, and I was home from college the month he turned fifteen. I noticed our father noticing things too: Manoj flipping his phone face down at dinner, going to the terrace to take calls, saying "just friends" and nothing more.
One evening Papa didn't grab the phone or demand passwords. He sat on the terrace steps next to Manoj and asked, "Who are these friends? Tell me about one of them."
Manoj shrugged, then said something about a boy from the football club. I couldn't hear all of it.
Then Papa said, "You don't have to tell me everything. But two rules: you never meet anyone from online without telling us, and if anything online scares you, you come to me. No trouble for telling."
I don't know what Manoj felt. But the next week I saw him show Papa a funny video from the football group.

qa.q: Where did Manoj go to take calls?
qa.a: Manoj went to the terrace to take calls.

qa.q: What might Papa have been feeling when he noticed the phone face down?
qa.a: Papa was likely worried, sensing secrecy, but calm enough to choose curiosity instead of demanding passwords.

qa.q: What made Papa's approach work better than an interrogation?
qa.a: He asked an open question, respected Manoj's privacy, and set two clear safety rules with a promise of no trouble for telling.

qa.q: How might Manoj see his father's approach?
qa.a: Manoj probably felt respected rather than accused, which may be why he later shared a video from the football group.

grounding: An observer sees a parent meet a teenager's secrecy with open questions and clear safety expectations, not interrogation.

subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage:
Monday. Uma noticed that Pradeep, fifteen, now closed his laptop whenever she walked in, and laughed at messages he wouldn't explain. Her chest tightened. Who was he talking to?
Wednesday. She almost did it: took his phone off the table, ready to read. Then she put it back. She remembered how she'd hidden her own diary from her mother at his age.
That night she knocked on his door. "Can I sit? I'm curious about your friends. Who makes you laugh like that?"
He hesitated. "Some people from the chess server. We play online."
"Tell me about the best player."
He talked for ten minutes.
Next Sunday. At breakfast she said, "I trust you. My only rules: no sharing your address or photos with people online, never meet anyone without telling us, and if anyone makes you uncomfortable, you tell me. You won't be in trouble."
Pradeep nodded. "Okay, Ma. Fair."

qa.q: What does Pradeep play with people online?
qa.a: He plays chess on a chess server.

qa.q: What was Uma worried about on Monday?
qa.a: Uma felt anxious, her chest tightening, wondering who Pradeep was talking to and why he hid it.

qa.q: Which of Uma's choices built trust, and why?
qa.a: She put his phone back, asked open questions about his friends, then set clear safety rules without accusation, so Pradeep felt respected.

qa.q: How did Pradeep experience Uma's approach?
qa.a: Pradeep felt trusted rather than suspected, enough to talk for ten minutes and call the rules fair.

grounding: A parent senses a teenager's online secrecy and responds with open questions and clear safety expectations, not interrogation.

passage:
"Ritu, your Papa was fifteen once too, you know. Let your Uday Dada tell you.
"He started coming home late from tuition, saying 'with friends', and nothing else. His phone was always hidden in his pocket. Your Dadi wanted to check it every night. I wanted to shout.
"I was so worried I couldn't sleep. But I remembered how my own father searched my school bag and how much I hated him for it.
"So one evening I took him for a walk to the lake and asked, 'Who are your friends? What do you do after tuition?' He was quiet, then told me: a group of boys practising in a garage band. He was scared we'd say music was a waste of time.
"I said, 'Fine. Tell us where you are, be home by nine, and never go anywhere with someone you met online without telling us.'
"He agreed. And you know what? He still plays the guitar.

qa.q: Where did Uday Dada take Ritu's Papa to talk?
qa.a: He took him for a walk to the lake.

qa.q: What was Uday Dada feeling when his son started hiding things?
qa.a: He felt so worried he couldn't sleep, and was angry enough to want to shout.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Choosing a calm walk and open questions instead of searching the phone let the son admit the band, and clear rules kept him safe.

qa.q: Why had Ritu's Papa been hiding things at fifteen?
qa.a: He was scared his parents would say music was a waste of time, so hiding the garage band felt safer.

grounding: An elder recalls sensing a teenager's secrecy and responding with open questions and clear safety rules, not searching.

subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage: Nirmala had twenty minutes before her night shift at the hospital, and the bus would not wait. But Dolma had flipped her phone face down again the moment Nirmala walked in, the third time that week, and a new name kept lighting up: "K". Nirmala's chest tightened. A dozen questions crowded her mouth: Who is K? Show me. Since when? She took a breath and sat on the edge of the bed instead. "I noticed the phone flips. You're allowed private things, Dolma. I'm your mother, not a detective. I won't grab it." Dolma's shoulders stayed up. "But my two rules stand: nobody online asks you to keep secrets from me, and you don't meet anyone you only know from the phone. Deal?" Dolma looked at her a long moment. "K is Karma from basketball camp. We're... talking." She went pink. "Okay," Nirmala said, grabbing her bag. "Tell me about Karma tomorrow, if you want."

qa.q: How long did Nirmala have before her night shift?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling when Dolma flipped the phone face down?
qa.a: Nirmala felt anxious, her chest tightening as a dozen worried questions crowded in.

qa.q: Which part of Nirmala's approach balanced privacy and safety?
qa.a: She named what she noticed, promised not to grab the phone, and restated two clear safety rules about secrets and meetings instead of interrogating.

qa.q: How might Dolma have felt when Nirmala promised not to grab the phone?
qa.a: Dolma was guarded at first, but being trusted with privacy and given clear rules made it safe enough to say who K was.

grounding: Shows a parent sensing a teenager's secrecy about her phone and answering the worry with open words and clear safety expectations rather than interrogation.
